articles.title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
articles.summary: Det Supt Andy Furphy said he hoped other potential victims would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.
body: Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court
Warning: Details of rape and sexual assault
Russell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.
The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.
More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.
Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.
Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand had initially been coy and quiet in police interviews, said Furphy, but became bolder as officers continued to question him.
"As he gets used to something, he becomes more emboldened by it," Furphy said. "You can certainly see that in his offending."

Hundreds of people were interviewed as part of the investigation and officers said several witnesses came forward, some of whom had previously had a sexual relationship with Brand. Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed.
Brand, 51, who was described in court as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator", was once one of the UK's most high-profile and in-demand entertainers.
Some of the women said they had been left "haunted for years" by what he did to them.
Speaking to the BBC, officers working on the three-year Metropolitan Police investigation described how bringing Brand to justice was not without its challenges.
Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed by police as part of the investigation
Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.
The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.
The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke.
"We kind of assumed that people might want to come forward," Furphy said, "and people came forward."

Victim reports were made to forces across the country and the Met set up a dedicated team of officers to lead the investigation, which it called Operation Actinolite. Officers said they have since taken more than 340 witness statements - including from Brand's former employers, his ex-colleagues and associates.
One officer was assigned to read Brand's books, watch his stand-up routines and DVDs and listen to his podcasts to help build the case.
Brand's high profile and the intense media scrutiny around him proved a challenge to officers, said Furphy.
Another complexity for the team was the allegations were all "non-recent". The earliest dated back 27 years. It meant there was no CCTV and no forensic evidence to work with.
Furphy said police had to look for other ways to build their case.

"Can we look at where the victims were at the time? Who did they speak to in the aftermath of it? Did they tell anybody else? What other available material is there for us to review that might lend some weight to it? Just because it's non-recent doesn't mean that we can't solve it at all."
A former friend of Brand's was called to court to give evidence for the prosecution, while a statement from the parents of one of the women was heard.
The entertainer's former personal assistant, who worked closely with Brand, told the jury about his "insane sexual appetite".
Two months after the police investigation began, Brand was interviewed under caution for the first time. He was interviewed on two further occasions in the following months.

In each interview he provided officers with a prepared statement, which said he did not recognise the complainants or recall the alleged incidents and that if any sexual activity had taken place, it would have been consensual. He then answered "no comment" to the officers' questions.

Charges were brought against Brand in early April 2025: one count of rape, one count of oral rape, two charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault. The final charge would later be changed to attempted indecent assault at his trial.
The charges all related to women who had come forward since the initial Channel 4 documentary.

The following month he appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, in London. He was swarmed by camera crews, so much so that it took him more than two minutes to walk the short distance to the court door. At a later court hearing he pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Meanwhile, women continued to come forward with more allegations.
In July 2025, Brand was interviewed for a fourth time before being charged with further offences: one count of rape and one count of sexual assault. He also denied those allegations.
And then on 14 October 2026, accompanied by his wife Laura, the actor and comedian entered the glass dock at London's Southwark Crown Court for the start of his trial.
Brand arrives at court ahead of his trial, accompanied by his wife Laura
The women each came to court and gave evidence to the jury from behind a screen, with Brand listening from the dock. At times they cried as they gave their evidence.
Furphy believes there may be more women who will now come forward.

"I think it's likely - potentially - that other women will come forward," he said. "They'll probably gain some courage and some confidence from what's happened in the courtroom over the last few weeks."

He credits the women for their bravery during what has been at times a "deeply uncomfortable" process. "They are courageous, determined women and our focus has always been on them, not Russell Brand."

articles.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
articles.summary: The widow of ER creator Michael Crichton argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the 1990s series.
body: Noah Wyle stars in The Pitt, the medical series set in a Pittsburgh emergency room that first aired in 2025
US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.
The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.
Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.

A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.

Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.
"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.
It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.
But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.
The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.
Noah Wyle (second right) previously starred in ER alongside Anthony Edwards, George Clooney and Eriq La Salle
ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.
The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.
Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.
Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.

But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series.
They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs".
Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.

After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".
But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim.
Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".

The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events.

Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."
Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

articles.title: Pope Leo hosts Bob Dylan at official residence in Rome
articles.summary: Pope Leo had previously quoted Dylan's work in the preface of a book warning against nuclear rearmament.
body: The two Americans met during Dylan's tour of Italy
Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.

The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
body: With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results
ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

articles.title: Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me
articles.summary: Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to find out if she would inherit her father's condition.
body: Laura Sides faced a dilemma of whether to get tested to see if she had inherited her father's condition
If you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?
This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.
Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.

Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him.

"We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. "I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."
Laura had just celebrated her 21st birthday when she began caring for her dad
It was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant".
"All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."
Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died.
"All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.
It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013.
He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said.
"I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."
'Toss of a coin’ if I’d inherit dementia gene
As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling.
"There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.
After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous".
She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone.
"I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'"
She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there".
"I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."
The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"
Laura has taken part in medical trials all over the world
Laura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."
However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis.
"It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."
Laura (right) is a chef and owns a cafe restaurant and catering business with two friends
Laura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms.
"I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."
She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard.
"Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them?
"And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends."
However she says she has been "proven wrong".
"I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".
Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother.
"[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."
Laura loves swimming and is aiming to swim in as many seas as possible
For Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy".
"It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe.
"I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but...I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things.
"I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."

articles.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary: The trial was condemned as "unethical" and "neocolonial" because half of the babies would not be given the vaccine.
body: Like many neighbouring countries, Guinea-Bissau waits until babies are six weeks old to vaccinate them against hepatitis B, while the WHO says it should be done at birth (file photo)
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".
The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.
Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.
The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.

Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.
The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.
The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.
It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.
Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.
Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.

Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.
But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.
The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.
Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.
He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.
"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."
He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.
Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.
Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.
The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.
"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.
Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.

Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.

Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.
"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."
The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.
Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.
"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.
His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.
SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.
The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.
Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.
He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.
Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.
He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.
On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.
Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.
They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.
The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.
Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.
The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.

Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.
Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.

Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.
There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

articles.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
articles.summary: As South Africans vote in local elections, residents tell the BBC they are tired of the poor quality of services they get.
body: More than 500 parties are contesting the elections
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Election officials say voting is going smoothly, despite long queues at some polling stations.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.

For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.

The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.

Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
Can this man broaden the appeal of a South African party seen by some as 'too white'?
South Africa's political marriage of convenience avoids divorce - just
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.

A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".

"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.

Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.

The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.

The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.

These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.
Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.

Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.

articles.title: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital
articles.summary: Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital
body: A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.

Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.”

A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja.

People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK previously. A case in 1976 was from a laboratory needle incident, and the three others involved health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

articles.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis
articles.summary: Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse
body: Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.
Related: Madame Lynch: how an Irish woman joined the ranks of Paraguay’s heroes
In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.

Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.

The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.

The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.

Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.
Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.

“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.
Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.
“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.

“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.

Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.

Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.
Vice-President Pedro Alliana automatically assumes the presidency to complete the constitutional term until August 2028.

About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

articles.title: Bomb threats disrupt at least 25 flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears
articles.summary: Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel
body: Hoax bomb threats have caused at least 25 flights across Europe to be disrupted, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.
The series of warnings on Thursday affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.

The threats affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious.

In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.
The Met said threats had been made against four aircraft departing from or arriving at Heathrow. A police spokesperson added that, after an assessment, “no security issues [were] identified”.

The day of hoaxes followed similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance. In total at least 33 flights have been affected this week.

Investigators said on Thursday there remained no evidence that the hoaxes were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, although inquiries across Europe into the incidents continue.

The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.
The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma, which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse.

Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov. On his Telegram channel Pozdnyakov, a prominent supporter of the war in Ukraine, did not comment on or claim responsibility for the bomb threats.

The emails reportedly read: “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this for ever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”

A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the airport had received an anonymous threat by phone on Thursday morning, causing a flight to be delayed. It was understood to be a Ryanair flight from London Stansted.
A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels-Charleroi was inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard toilet.
The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.
The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems.
Related: Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?

A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

In Rome, Guido Crosetto, the Italian defence minister, said: “It seems to me that every day now, from refrigerators to blood supplies in France, to these fake alarms, there’s someone who has an interest in stoking tensions.”
Asked if he knew who was behind the hoaxes, he said: “It’s called ‘under-threshold warfare’ because it’s below the attribution threshold. It’s done that way on purpose, so no one can pin the blame.”
Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.
Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.

Capt Martin Drake, a former airline pilot and technical adviser to the British Airline Pilots’ Association union, said airlines had security teams who assessed each threat on a traffic-light scale: green to keep going or red to be grounded, with an amber option only for flights yet to take off, allowing tighter checks and searches of the plane before clearing it to fly.

“If you want to deliberately disrupt a flight, then you need to do so once it’s airborne,” said Drake. Pilots have a QRH – a quick response handbook – whose instructions will probably include to descend quickly as well as divert to the nearest airport on receipt of a red alert.
At cruising altitude, “aircraft pressurisation would do a lot of the work of any improvised explosive device”.

While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.
Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.

He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer in Amsterdam and Angela Giuffrida in Rome

articles.title: Herzog to meet Israeli election rivals as decision nears on path to power
articles.summary: President calls on all parties to help avoid new election after Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fell short of majority
body: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, was due to meet Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, on Thursday with less than a week left before he decides which of the two men should first try to form a government.

A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.

Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.
“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.

Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.
Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.

“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility ​rests upon us,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu remains prime minister ​in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another ‌election, which must be held if no candidate ‌succeeds.

Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on ​an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast ​doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing ​the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said ​on Wednesday that the election’s integrity ‌had not been compromised. The ​head of the committee, the supreme court justice ​Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

articles.title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry
articles.summary: Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect
body: The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.
More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.
He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.
Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.
Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”
He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.
Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.
Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

articles.title: ‘Sick to my stomach’: trans Americans on politicians who spent $183m attacking them for votes
articles.summary: Republicans spent big on midterms ads about transgender issues – and some Democratic candidates parroted anti-trans messaging, too
body: Metal Hennessy, a 19-year-old trans man who lives in Kansas, quoted one of his state’s most enduring exports – The Wizard of Oz – when describing the defeat of Roger Marshall, the incumbent Republican senator, on Tuesday: “Ding dong, the witch is dead.”
Related: Washington state passes ballot measure banning trans girls from school sports

This US midterm season, Kansans like Hennessy were subjected to a wave of anti-trans attacks as Marshall attempted to fight off a challenge from Democratic and Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton. The AP reported that Republicans pumped $7m into related ads, which aired 7,000 times in the state.

Hennessy was not surprised that Republicans would target his community to win votes – earlier this year, a law took effect invalidating the drivers licenses of trans people in the state and requiring them to use bathrooms in government buildings associated with their sex assigned at birth. Nor was Hennessy surprised the strategy failed.
“I don’t think trans issues are a swing issue to the average cis-het population. Most people are concerned about gas prices or the economy,” he said.

In the weeks leading up to Tuesday, Republicans spent an estimated $183m on ads about transgender issues. Elon Musk poured millions into political groups that attacked trans rights, intensely targeting Democrat James Talarico’s Senate run in Texas. Trump, who successfully leveraged the culture war issue in 2024, stumped on it again, calling gender affirming care “mutilization” (meaning “mutilation”). Conservative candidates actively campaigned on the platform, calling their liberal opponents supporters of an overly woke agenda.

“Prior to election day,” said Zein Murib, an associate professor of political science at Fordham University, “there was a lot of concern in trans rights circles that whatever way the races broke for certain candidates who had taken up anti-trans messaging would signal that was a winning strategy.”

But Texas and Kansas – along with the US Senate and House – flipped blue. Alabama elected its first transgender lawmaker, Allison Montgomery, an incoming state representative, despite her Republican challenger’s incendiary comments about her identity. Five other states – Georgia, Washington, Wisconsin, Michigan and Florida – elected trans and non-binary candidates at the state level for the first time.
“I think this is probably as positive of an outcome that we could expect at this moment,” said Murib.

The “blue wave” can be seen as a repudiation of the Trump administration’s most divisive policies: violent immigration enforcement, the war in Iran, economically devastating tariffs. Some trans Americans also see it as a repudiation of his party’s aggressive rhetoric.

Republicans’ anti-trans ads were “a huge waste of money”, said Verniss McFarland, founder and executive director of The Mahogany Project, a Black-led nonprofit dedicated to supporting the trans and gender-expansive community in Houston, Texas. Wulf James, 41, a Two Spirit Indigenous person who lives in Kansas, called the ads a “fear-mongering exercise”. “There have always been trans and queer people, and no amount of big spending is going to change that,” they said.

Soraya Sobreidad, 67, an artist who lives in New York, said the ads were “something that the Republicans thought up to use as a way to weaponize and take the focus off of bigger issues”, and pointed out that only 1% of Americans aged 13 and up are transgender.

“Multimillions of dollars are being invested to spread false narratives about trans people,” she said. “That’s just a fraction of dollars that gets invested back into the community. [Trans] lives shouldn’t be strictly experienced around somber moments, anti-trans policies, or political ads. Trans people, and especially Black trans people, should experience life in totality.”

It wasn’t just Republicans. Indeed, some Democratic candidates parroted anti-trans messaging and won their midterms races. Josh Turek, the incoming Iowa senator, released an ad saying he was against “males competing in female sports” and “taxpayers paying for sex changes.” (Turek said he released the ad to respond to false claims put forth by his Republican challenger.) In Ohio, Marcy Kaptur, the incumbent representative, flaunted that she voted “with Republicans” to keep “transgender ideologies out of schools”. Kathy Castor, in Florida’s 14th congressional district, also said she did not believe “biological males” should take part in girls’ sports.

“Instead of guiding the public toward an attitude that could be more accepting, some Democrats capitulated,” said Andrew R Flores, an associate professor of government at American University. “To me, the indictment is: where do we go now, so the Democratic party doesn’t feel like it needs to follow [Republicans] on this issue?”

Murib pointed to Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan senator-elect who reiterated support for trans rights during a 60 Minutes interview the Sunday before the election. “He wasn’t going to throw trans people under the bus,” Murib said. “Democrats need to stick with that to be different. They can’t just go further right on the issue like the Republicans and some of their colleagues have done.”
No matter where the rhetoric comes from on the political spectrum, it has real life consequences, say trans Americans.

Jane, a 20-year-old Kansas college student, felt an “aura” around the state because of the influx of anti-trans ads. “Because of those ads, it’s much harder for me to live my life,” Jane said. “Nobody’s attacked me or called me names. But you can tell that you’re being watched constantly, or judged silently. I don’t think that’s a particularly new phenomenon for trans people, but the midterms are not helping much.” (Jane did not want their last name printed out of safety concerns.)

Max Mowitz, executive director of One Iowa, the state’s largest LGBTQ+ organization, has complicated feelings about being expected to support a Democratic candidate such as Turek simply because they had no better option. “It’s been very hard to constantly need to center the fact that trans people are humans,” Mowitz said. “It can sometimes feel delusional to be hopeful and optimistic, but I would rather be delusional than to just give up.”

Shira Berkowitz, the senior director of public policy at PROMO Missouri, an LGBTQ+ advocacy organization, described feeling “sick to my stomach” because of anti-trans attacks. But they also described a recent encounter that buoyed their spirits: two of their group’s canvassers knocked on the door of an older couple who was not interested in talking about trans issues. As the canvassers walked away, a car drove up and out climbed a gender-expansive teenager – the couple’s child – who noticed the canvassers’ rainbow lanyards. The teen asked the canvassers to come back.
“They returned to the door together and had this conversation where they witnessed their parents’ hearts expanding a little,” Berkowitz said. “It is possible to change somebody’s heart and mind.”
On Tuesday, Berkowitz’s home state, which is reliably red, voted to protect abortion rights and gender-affirming care for minors.
Americans have bigger issues, and trans people have bigger issues, too

Despite positive developments this election season, trans Americans still face bigotry and a deeply transphobic presidential administration. The day after Trump won the 2024 election, The Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention for LGBTQ+ youth, reported a 700% increase in calls, texts, and messages to its crisis hotline. There are 154 national anti-trans bills under consideration in the US, with 63 passing in 2026. Various states have restricted access to gender affirming care for minors and banned transgender athletes from competing on teams that do not match their sex at birth.

While trans issues were far from the top election issue for the vast majority of voters – not compared to cost of living, government corruption and immigration – polling from Pew Research found that 73% of US adults are uncomfortable with transgender athletes competing on sports teams that match their gender identity. This sentiment was borne out in some state midterms elections. Arizona approved a ballot measure expanding the state’s ban on trans athletes; Nebraska voters added a ban to the state’s constitution. Washington passed a sports ban that requires girls to undergo “medical testing” to prove their sex via genital check or hormone test. (Colorado’s sports ban is too early to call but looks likely to pass.)
Critics call these laws unnecessary and discriminatory, while advocates say they make sports “fair” for girls.

Murib, the Fordham professor, said that discourse around trans sports bans “manufactures this idea that women and girls are in need of protection”. “This is the product of over 40 years of rightwing mobilization to create a logic in which the gender binary is considered natural and unquestionable,” they added.

Hennessy, the 19-year-old trans Kansan, went to bed early on election night. They woke up to results that made them feel vindicated – and laser-focused on kitchen table issues such as the cost of living and stalled job market.

“Americans have bigger issues, and trans people have bigger issues, too,” they said. “As a trans person, there is more to worry about than bathroom bans and other laws that unfortunately affect my day-to-day life. Like, we all gotta eat. Let’s celebrate for like the next 28 hours and then let’s get to work.”

articles.title: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?
articles.summary: With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans?
body: More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week, with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe.
What do we know so far, and how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

At least 35 flights have been disrupted this week, beginning on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest. Thursday’s threats affected airports in London, Birmingham, Brussels, Bucharest, Madrid, Milan, Prague, Rome, Sofia and Warsaw, among others.
So far all incidents have been confirmed to be false alarms, with nothing suspicious found by relevant security authorities.

There is no clear pattern of airports and airlines targeted, although a significant number have involved Italian airports as an origin or destination. Seven flights this week were to – or from the UK – and four to or from Ireland.
Sofia and Milan each recorded six incidents, followed by Rome (five) and Prague (four). Ryanair was the hardest-hit airline, with eight reported cases.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said on Thursday it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked”. He stressed: “Any threats against civilians are unacceptable.”
There is no intelligence yet pointing to any particular group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, amid growing concerns over hybrid incidents targeting Europe.
Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but the multiplicity of this week’s threats is unusual.

As our transport correspondent, Gwyn Topham, notes on our live blog, the ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means a hoaxer now has a level of detail about schedules and a plane’s type and technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.
Little is known about how these threats were reported to airlines or relevant authorities, though in cases involving Bulgaria, Italy, Poland and Spain they were reportedly sent via email.

The Italian news agency Ansa, citing police sources, said the warning for Helsinki-Rome and Dublin-Rome flights came from an anonymous email written in Italian and sent to the Rome airport company ADR and other affiliated companies early on Thursday.

Another anonymous email in Italian was sent to Milan Malpensa airport, claiming that explosive devices were on flights from Thessaloniki and Porto. The email included the flight numbers, the airline names and their landing times in Milan, Ansa said.

Most authorities issued carefully worded statements confirming their security checks on the affected planes. However, the Czech police – which investigated four planes landing at Václav Havel airport in Prague on Thursday – said they considered the reports of “low relevance”.
Relevant national authorities treat these incidents seriously in line with their safety procedures, with reports of fighter jet escorts in Bulgaria, France, Hungary and Italy.
Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

Joji Waites, the director of flight safety at the British Airline Pilots’ Association (Balpa), said any threat received by an airline was passed to a team of assessors who would grade it “red”, meaning credible, “amber”, partly credible, or “green”, not credible. If the plane is already in the air, the only rating possible is red or green.
He said: “Usually if a plane is still on the Tarmac that will mean an evacuation, and if it is in the air the priority will be to land the plane as soon and as safely as possible.”
Airlines appear to be concerned about the scale of possible disruptions and worry potential copycat alerts could cause further chaos.

Wizz Air acknowledged “a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days”. It said: “Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks.”

Finnair, which had two planes affected, said: “Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when also other airlines in Europe have faced hoax bomb threats.” It added: “Threats are almost always unfounded.”

articles.title: Protesters march in cities across France as unions stage general strike
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands demonstrate over cost of living and cuts to public services as 70,000 police officers deployed
body: Hundreds of thousands of people have marched in cities across France in the latest round of street demonstrations, as trade unions put pressure on the government with a general strike over the cost of living and cuts to public services.

Striking teachers, hospital staff and rail workers joined high school and university students in largely peaceful demonstrations in Paris and other cities on Thursday amid a high police presence of 70,000 officers.
The government estimated that at least 600,000 people had taken part, while the leftwing CGT trade union put the figure at almost 1.6 million.

Riot police fired teargas at the end of demonstrations in Bordeaux and Lyon. In Paris, police prevented schoolchildren from setting up barricades with wheelie bins outside high schools across the city in the early morning.
In the east of the city, police used teargas to prevent students from accessing the Hélène Boucher high school.

“This is a historic protest movement but the government’s only real response has been to seriously crack down on it with police, so we had to come out on to the street today,” said Rebecca, 30, a social worker for children with disabilities from Paris’s southern suburbs. “There are police everywhere, but where is the funding for other public services?”
Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor learning conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests.
Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.

France’s four main rail unions said the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.

Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 election to replace Macron next spring.

High school students, who have been protesting for weeks, continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. The government said 81 high schools were affected on Thursday, while students’ unions put the number at 1,000.

University students joined in blockading faculties, with a third of higher education sites affected, the government said. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined strikes, with private school teacher unions taking part alongside state school teachers.

At the Paris demonstration, a 46-year-old psychiatric nurse from the city’s south-eastern suburbs said: “We’ve got to protect public services. Hospital cuts are impacting the work we try to do with psychiatric patients.
“There are fewer doctors and nurses. People are overworked and fatigued. It’s hard to make ends meet on salaries that haven’t properly been reviewed for years.”
A Paris train driver with the CGT union said: “It’s important that we also come out to demonstrate against the rise of the far right as the presidential election approaches.”
Rights groups protested over what they said was heavy-handed policing and an attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.

The Ligue des droits de l’Homme (French human rights league) said this week there had been an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice”, as authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres as well as curfews in certain areas.

Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time, with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government.” She criticised decisions by authorities in some cities to push demonstrations out of city centres.
As the protests were under way, the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced a meeting to be held next Monday with trade unions and business leaders to discuss salaries and the cost of living.

articles.title: EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students
articles.summary: Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say
body: The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.
