At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.

These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.

But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

The EU wants a return to the pre-Brexit status quo where European students paid the UK domestic rate of university tuition, rather than international fees, which can be about four to six times higher for an undergraduate degree.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing an agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

But at least six member states, including in central and eastern Europe, want the university fees issue settled by the summit, while many are seeking a firmer commitment on the issue from the British government, according to four EU sources.
Related: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme

One EU diplomat told the Guardian: “Having a youth experience scheme without an agreement on tuition fees has very little added value,” noting the much lower cost of university education in many EU countries and therefore potential greater advantage to British students.
A second EU diplomat said there was cautious optimism about the November summit, but “a large majority” wanted “a more convincing British commitment” on tuition fees.

A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on leaks or provide a running commentary on live negotiations. We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

For the EU, the creation of a youth experience scheme, known as Yes, which will enable those aged 18 to 30 to live, work and study on both sides of the Channel is a high priority. The erosion of people-to-people links is seen as one of the big losses of Brexit, and many European officials studied in the UK, making the issue especially resonant.

EU officials argue the bloc has leverage, saying the food and drink deal – a Labour manifesto pledge estimated to be worth £5.1bn a year to the British economy – would come into force only if there was a satisfactory agreement on tuition fees.

Similarly, the agreement to relink emissions trading systems sundered by Brexit, which would protect British exporters from European carbon taxes, could also be delayed pending agreement on tuition fees.
A leaked version of the summit statement hints at the link between the trio of agreements, looking forward to “their joint and timely entry into force”.

Separately, EU sources have suggested without a deal on tuition fees, the EU could delay talks on British reintegration into the European electricity market that are expected to intensify next year. To secure its return to the market, the UK would have to pledge an “appropriate” contribution to European cohesion funds aimed at boosting economic development in poorer regions.

This week the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.
The EU said there would be no deal on Made in Europe at the November summit because the bloc was still finalising its position on the key draft law, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
Targeted at strategic industrial sectors, such as electric cars and renewables, the law would mean public subsidies and contracts would only go towards products made in Europe.

France, supported by many lawmakers in the European parliament, is pushing for a narrow definition of Made in Europe, while Germany leads a larger group of countries that don’t want to exclude trade partners including the UK.

While Britain is keen to resolve the issue, EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the IAA text until next spring. In a significant milestone, France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK, but it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA such as renewables and nuclear technology, or other draft proposals aimed at promoting European preference.

In a win for the UK, the draft summit statement proposes a “trusted partnership” on strategic industries, starting with steel and defence. The aim is to stop either side becoming collateral damage of the other’s trade defence measures targeted at China’s heavily subsidised imports.

articles.title: Russia agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter missile launchers
articles.summary: Leaked documents offer insight into Russian-Iranian military cooperation as US weighs up next steps in Iran war
body: Russia arranged to supply Iran with 90 launchers for advanced guided missiles, according to leaked defence industry documents that shed light on the depth of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.

The documents, obtained by Dallas Analytics, a Ukrainian private intelligence firm, and shared with the Guardian, detail plans to supply Iran with launchers for the LMUR, a guided missile fired from attack helicopters which Russian forces have used extensively against Ukrainian targets since the full-scale invasion in 2022.

A production schedule drawn up in May 2024 by Vympel, a leading Russian designer of missiles and launch systems, lists an order for 90 launchers under an export contract designated “K-10”, with deliveries scheduled between late 2024 and December 2025. Separate internal paperwork explicitly identifies K-10 as Iran.

The records do not establish whether the launchers were ultimately delivered. However, a separate production schedule listing six Yak-130 jet trainers destined for Iran in 2023 is consistent with publicly reported deliveries of the aircraft.
The files offer fresh insight into Russian-Iranian military cooperation at a sensitive moment as Washington weighs its next steps in its war against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Observers widely regard Moscow as one of the main winners of a prolonged war in Iran, which has brought Russia strategic and economic advantages.

Russia has benefited from an increase in global energy prices triggered by disruptions to shipping through the strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure across the Gulf. Higher oil revenues give the Kremlin an additional source of funds for its war in Ukraine and could help ease pressure on Russia’s strained budget.
The war has also diverted international attention and western military resources away from Ukraine, further straining Kyiv’s access to crucial US-made Patriot air defence interceptors.

Donald Trump has repeatedly played down the extent of Moscow’s support for Iran. Last month, the US president wrote that Russia was doing “very little, if anything” to help Tehran, arguing that he did not want to drive Moscow away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
Related: As Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?
Trump’s claims contrast with European intelligence findings that Russia has provided Iran with key data and satellite images that could help it target US forces in the Middle East.
European intelligence agencies have also warned that Moscow was preparing to supply Tehran with explosive-laden drones for use against the US and Israel.

Military cooperation between Russia and Iran has expanded significantly since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when Tehran became a crucial supplier of Shahed attack drones, which Russia has since begun manufacturing domestically.

Moscow has denied reports that it is supplying military equipment to Iran for use in the current conflict. The two countries signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2025 that includes provisions for countering shared threats, although it stops short of the mutual defence commitments contained in Russia’s security pact with North Korea.
But Tehran and Moscow have kept in very close cooperation in recent months.
In October alone, senior Russian and Iranian officials held three high-level meetings, underscoring the growing importance both governments attach to their relationship.

Moscow has been careful not to publicise its military cooperation with Tehran, wary of jeopardising Putin’s relationship with Trump. Russia also faces constraints on its ability to supply Iran with weapons, with much of its military production already stretched by the demands of the war in Ukraine.

The leaked documents provide a glimpse into the pressures facing Russia’s defence industry. In the May 2024 letter, Vympel warned that delays in the supply of essential components threatened the assembly of missile launchers and risked disrupting Russian state defence contracts.

articles.title: UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
articles.summary: Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’
body: The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.

Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.

The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly after the US consulate strongly condemned the sentence on Thursday, China warned “relevant parties” to “stop making irresponsible remarks” about Hong Kong judicial cases.
Human rights groups and politicians from across the political spectrum also criticised the sentence.
Related: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director for Amnesty International, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
She said the new conviction “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction”.
Wong has already spent six years in detention and had been due for release in January 2027.

In the most recent Foreign Office report on Hong Kong, published last month, the UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said that Wong’s case “reinforced concerns about the increasingly broad application of national security legislation”.
Wong’s supporters called on governments around the world to push for his release.

Nathan Law, a Hong Kong activist and friend of Wong’s who was named as a co-conspirator in the case, said: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.”
Law called the sentencing “a farce” which signified that China “is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil”.
When former British colony Hong Kong was handed to China in 1997, it was promised 50 years of “one country two systems”, under which the city would keep some autonomy and freedoms.
The UK considers Beijing to be in violation of that international treaty, after the crackdown on protests in 2019 and 2020, and the sweeping legal reforms that followed.
Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith said Wong had “stood up” for that treaty, which he said China had “subsequently trashed”.
He added: “Despite this, the UK government has done little to nothing about it. The more we give in when China breaks the rules, the worse it gets in the future.”

The Labour MP James Naish said: “Hongkongers in my constituency chose Britain for the freedoms Joshua is jailed for defending – values we should all support. This is not a lenient sentence and the government must show China that Britain will not tolerate it.”

articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war
articles.summary: Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power
body: The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.

A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
Reuters reported on Monday that Houthi forces were only about 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government.
A burst of government dismissals and appointments reflects military reverses and possibly a perceived need to be more sensitive to the demands of southern Yemenis.

Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided in two, and there is a strong movement built around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeking to revert to that division, or create a more federated country.
The government has become dependent on southern troops to fend off Houthi advances, but these forces insist they will fight only to defend land inside former South Yemen.

Fresh claims were also aired this week that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organisation against their will. The growing criticism of Saudi Arabia from STC officials in the media reflects their confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will have to let the STC operate openly. Not all southern separatists support the STC, an organisation that overreached itself in January, making it easier for the Saudi leadership to defer decisions on the southern question.

Some of the most senior figures in the UN-backed government are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen and the government is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries. Critics say the administration has become a “hotel government”.
Related: Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?

Earlier this week, its ruling executive – the presidential leadership council – met for the first time in months in Riyadh, where it addressed the loss of swathes of territory to the Houthis along Yemen’s west coast. Since then, the fighting has moved into the mountains around Taiz.

In an attempt to rebalance the north-south divide in his government, President Rashad al-Alimi sacked the long-serving information minister, Muammar al-Eryani, replacing him with Prof Salem al-Awlaki, previously a minister for the civil service and a spokesperson for the STC from 2017 to 2019. Alimi chose two other southerners as ministers for local administration and the civil service and appointed new leaders for the civil aviation authority, the ports of Aden and the ministry of transport.

He also sacked Yusuf al-Sharaji, the military figure responsible for the Taiz front and Abu Bakr al-Jabouli, a brigadier responsible for the Tor al-Baha axis. Widespread accusations had been made about al-Sharaji’s failure to manage operations, resulting in the fall of several areas and districts to the Houthis.
The task of lifting the siege of Taiz and coordinating forces has been handed to Maj Gen Rashad al-Yousfi, a career officer.

Part of the difficulty is the tension between the different forces fighting on the government’s side. It has been claimed that Abu Zara’a, the leader of the Southern Giants, has fallen out with the Homeland Shield Forces, which are funded by Saudi Arabia and affiliated with Abdulrahman al-Lahji.

The Homeland Shield experienced heavy losses, leading al-Lahji to file an official report accusing Abu Zara’a of treason, and warning that the situation in Dhubab, close to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, had become extremely dangerous for the government. Repeated claims that control of the strait had been wrested back from the Houthis were contradicted by the evidence.

articles.title: ‘Wrong on every count’: How the Guardian reported the 1956 Suez crisis
articles.summary: The military conflict in Egypt involving the UK, France and Israel that ended with a humiliating exit for the two European nations
body: On 26 July 1956, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, the joint British-French enterprise which had owned and operated the canal since its construction in 1869. Both countries saw this as a threat to their interests and responded with a coordinated attack (with Israel) to take back the canal zone.

Israeli forces swept into the Sinai desert on 29 October and two days later there was an Anglo-French bombing campaign against Egyptian military targets. But on 6 November, under intense pressure from the international community and particularly the US, Britain and France accepted a UN-mandated ceasefire.

The Manchester Guardian was against the use of force from the beginning of the crisis. Under newly appointed editor Alastair Hetherington, the paper condemned an ultimatum given to the Egyptians to withdraw from the canal as “an act of folly without justification,” and on 5 November described the actions as “hideously miscalculated and utterly immoral”.

The Guardian’s critical coverage of the invasion proved so uncomfortable for the prime minister, Anthony Eden, that he tried to prevent the BBC from quoting from it and wanted the paper’s diplomatic correspondent, Richard Scott, banned from the airwaves. There was also strong public condemnation and as Guardian historian David Ayerst recorded, its reporters “often met with hostility as they went about their business.” In London, a plateglass window in the paper’s Fleet Street office was smashed.

President Nasser announced last night that the Egyptian government had decided to nationalise the Suez Canal Company and to use the income from the canal of $100m a year to build the Aswan high dam. Last week the United States and Britain withdrew their offers of money for the dam. Britain is the largest single shareholder in the Suez Canal Company, owning seven-sixteenths of the total. The company’s 99-year concession was due to expire in 13 years, after which the canal would have reverted to Egypt.Continue reading

Allied bombers made “concentrated attacks” last night on four Egyptian airfields, two near Cairo and two in the Suez canal zone. The RAF aircraft used were Vickers Valiants, the first of the V-class four-jet bombers, and English Electric Canberras. The targets of the attack were announced late last night. At the same time an Admiralty spokesman said that the cruiser Newfoundland, on shipping protection duties in the Gulf of Suez, had last night encountered an Egyptian frigate which failed to answer a challenge or to stop when called on to do so. She was therefore sunk and survivors taken on board the Newfoundland.Continue reading.

The world must be told clearly, as Mr Gaitskell said yesterday, that millions of British people are deeply shocked by the aggressive policy of the government. Its action in attacking Egypt is a disaster of the first magnitude. It is wrong on every count – moral, military, and political. It is a severe blow to Britain’s reputation, to the Atlantic alliance, to the United Nations, and, not least, to Britain’s prospect of material prosperity. To recover from the disaster will take years – if, indeed, it is ever possible. The government has ordered a military attack upon another country without just cause. Continue reading

Fighting ended in Egypt at midnight, in accordance with the ceasefire announced by the prime minister in the Commons six hours before. Allied troops advanced all day yesterday from Port Said, and at midnight were reported beyond Kantara, 30 miles to the south.

The prime minister said the ceasefire was subject to confirmation of acceptance by Egypt and Israel, and to Allied forces not being attacked. In New York the Secretary-General of the United Nations said he could give the required confirmation.

Asked by Mr Gaitskell whether there would be no further landing of Allied troops, the prime minister said there would be “no movement forward” from existing positions, but he could not exclude what was necessary “in supplies and troops of that kind.” Continue reading.
From our political correspondent7 November 1956

Last night, the government’s decision was examined coldly both by those who wanted Sir Anthony to go the whole hog in Egypt, and by those who wished the government had never started its adventure at all. Nobody supposes that the circumstances which have now led the government to order a ceasefire were the objectives which the government originally had in mind when the adventure started.

Some Tories were shaking their heads gloomily because they believe the Arab states would argue that Israel had beaten Egypt and that Egypt had beaten Britain (it remains to be seen whether the successes that have so far attended Egypt’s arms will really impress Arab opinion).
Related: Alan Rusbridger on the Suez crisis

Among the loyalists there is profound relief that the government has reversed the process of antagonising the United States. There is relief, too, that with Russia in a truculent mood Britain has taken a step to avoid the risk that her forces and equipment would be bogged down indefinitely in the Middle East. There is relief that Britain has ceased travelling away from the United Nations.

On 7 November 1956 the UN deployed an emergency force (UNEF) of peacekeepers into Egypt to halt the conflict. Egypt was granted ownership and sovereignty of the canal and in April 1957 it was re-opened to shipping.
Fears that Guardian’s editorial stance would lead to plummeting circulation were unfounded, with sales of the paper increasing, particularly in the south of the UK.

articles.title: What can Britain learn from backlash to Dutch slavery apology?
articles.summary: In the Netherlands many felt the move, while welcome, was mishandled and exclusionary, mirroring past inequality
body: Andy Burnham’s pledge to seek a “structured dialogue” with former colonies to help shape Britain’s first formal state apology for slavery marks the UK’s first tentative step down a path the Netherlands set out on five years ago.

The prime minister’s attempts to initiate a historic shift alongside the royal family – whose customary expressions of “profound personal sorrow”, falling short of an apology, was repeated by King Charles this week – echo a process begun by the Dutch state in 2021.

As London weighs its words, while firmly ruling out any support for reparations, the Dutch experience may provide a preview: in the Netherlands, apologising did not draw a line under the past for everyone, and prompted a political backlash, disillusion among many descendants, and a row over what justice really means.

That is not to say it was not the right thing to do. The apologies were “sensitive, the right words, the right gestures … You could feel the sincerity,” said Linda Nooitmeer, the then chair of the National Institute for the Study of Dutch Slavery and its Legacy (NiNsee).

It was about “restoring the humanity of the ancestors”, because a key historical element had been “the dehumanisation of people of African descent”, she said. “But when it comes to real change, the rights of people of African descent, we have another issue.”
Related: Repairing the legacy of slavery: what are campaigners calling for?

Merchants of the so-called Dutch Golden Age trafficked an estimated 600,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to brutal plantations in Suriname and Curaçao, as well as between 660,000 and 1 million across the Indian Ocean and East Indies.

By the 1770s, slavery-derived wealth generated more than 10% of the GDP of the province of Holland. Even the crown was enriched: Willems III, IV and V made what equates to €545m (£465m) in modern money from the trade between 1675 and 1770 alone.

The Netherlands was among the last European colonial powers to outlaw the practice, legally abolishing it in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean on 1 July 1863, 30 years after Britain and 15 after France. The actual end – freedom – came in 1873.
Afro-Surinamese and Afro-Caribbean community campaigners started demanding accountability in the 1980s. NiNsee was founded in 2002, and slavery entered the school curriculum in 2006.

The political trigger came in 2020, with the wave of protests that followed George Floyd’s murder in the US. If many had tried to ignore Dutch history, said the activist Patrick Mathurin at the time, “through our activism, we forced them to look”.

On 1 July 2021, Amsterdam’s mayor, Femke Halsema, broke ranks during the annual Dutch Keti Koti (“breaking the chains”) commemorations marking the anniversary of abolition, delivering a direct apology on behalf of the municipality.

Amsterdam’s involvement, Halsema said, had been “direct, worldwide, large-scale, multifaceted and protracted”, and the city’s immense past wealth and commercial legacy were “indivisible from persistent racism that still festers”.

Amsterdam’s apology was followed by those of Rotterdam, Utrecht and The Hague, and by the Dutch central bank. The then prime minister, Mark Rutte, who had insisted as late as 2020 that a national apology would only “polarise society”, began to waver.

In December 2022, Rutte delivered a landmark speech at the Dutch National Archives recognising slavery as a “crime against humanity” and admitting the Dutch state had “enabled, encouraged, and profited from slavery” for more than 250 years.

“Today, on behalf of the Dutch government, I apologise for the past actions of the Dutch state: posthumously to all enslaved people worldwide who suffered from those actions, to their daughters and sons, and to all their descendants down to the present day,” he said.
Related: UN votes to describe slave trade as ‘gravest crime against humanity’

Six months later, on 1 July 2023, in Amsterdam’s Oosterpark, King Willem-Alexander also asked forgiveness: “As your king, and as a member of the government, I make this apology myself. And I feel the weight of the words in my heart and my soul.”
Afterwards, however, there was anger among activists, advocacy groups and descendants, who criticised Rutte’s apology in particular as hasty, paternalistic and made without real consultation.

Roy Kaikusi Groenberg, of the Honour and Recovery Foundation, called the prime minister’s declaration a “neocolonial belch”. Caribbean intellectuals pointed out the obvious and painful irony of European politicians dictating the terms and timing of reconciliation.

While the Dutch government explicitly ruled out direct financial reparations to individuals or former colonies, it did back its apology with a €200m fund and an initial commitment towards a National Slavery Museum.

The money was divided between state-led educational and awareness programmes, such as overhauling school curriculums, funding historical research and preserving colonial heritage, and social initiatives and community grants to grassroots groups.

Nooitmeer, who has since set up Deeeni, a grassroots organisation focusing on economic initiatives in the African-origin community, said at the time there was a danger of apologies becoming the “mirrors and crystals of the 21st century”.

Mirrors and crystals, she noted, were the symbolic, empty trinkets with which enslaved people were once bought and sold. “Slavery was an economic system,” she says now. “If you say all this was wrong, when are you ready to talk about the economic side: reparations in the broader sense?”

Community ownership of the whole process “was completely lacking”, she said. While apologies might be made, “as long as the community is excluded from the decision-making process, the old mechanisms of inequality simply remain”.

A key lesson from the Dutch experience, Nooitmeer said, was that people of African descent today need some kind of “agency over what reparations should look like – and when they are considered sufficient”.
Related: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham

The Netherlands also witnessed a conservative political backlash. In 2021, only 31% of the Dutch public said they supported the idea of a national apology for slavery, said Sjoerd van Heck of Ipsos I&O, while 55% opposed it.

The numbers converged somewhat, reaching 38% in favour and 49% opposed in 2022 and, after the Rutte and Willem-Alexander apologies, 40% for versus 46% against, Van Heck said, but added: “It’s clear that the subject remained one that sharply divided the population.”

That was grist to the mill for Geert Wilders, who, like Europe’s other populist far-right leaders, has long ridiculed state apologies for past wrongs and pledged to rewrite school textbooks to emphasise their nation’s achievements. His Freedom party (PVV) won a shock victory in 2023 elections.
The National Slavery Museum, conceived with Surinamese, Caribbean and Dutch community participation and backed by €80m from Amsterdam city hall and the national government, is due to open in 2030.

But for Britain, the Dutch experience suggests that state apologies, while plainly welcome, may prove not so much a neat final settlement with colonial history as the opening of a new and almost certainly contested phase of reckoning.
