articles.title: How elderly ‘unsung heroes’ powered Lula’s historic fightback in Brazil
articles.summary: Older voters praised for helping tip balance in leftwing president’s favour against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff
body: It had been nearly a decade since Celia de Oliveira Soares last voted, and months since the 101-year-old great-grandmother last left her home.

But on 25 October, when Brazil held what many considered its most important presidential election in decades, relatives helped Soares into a wheelchair and drove her to a nearby school to make sure the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, did not prevail.
Soares clung to the banister as, step by step, she climbed two flights of stairs to the polling booth under the watchful eye of her granddaughter’s husband, Marcio Marques.
Inside, the frail but jaunty centenarian keyed the number “13” – representing Bolsonaro’s leftwing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – into an electronic voting machine and pressed confirm.
“I like Lula. I really do!” enthused Soares, a retired bank employee who has lived in Rio de Janeiro most of her life.

“I don’t like Bolsonaro or his father. So the efficient thing to do was go out and vote,” Soares added, as her grandsons, Tito and Ravi, played on the balcony around her surrounded by pot plants and books.
Soares is one of more than 1 million elderly people who, having missed the election’s 4 October first round – which Lula lost – decided to vote in the second.

Never since the return of democracy in the 1980s had the first-round loser bounced back, but Lula did just that. And after Lula’s shock revival, elderly voters have been hailed as the election’s unsung heroes – including by Lula himself.

At his 81st birthday party last week, the leftist veteran shed tears while describing his gratitude to the elderly people who helped him clinch a historic fourth term while clutching walking frames and sticks.

“I honestly think it was the most powerful and human image I’ve ever seen during an election,” Lula said of viral pictures showing voters in their 80s, 90s and 100s being carried into polling centres by relatives or carers, some in stretchers or wheelchairs.

In north-east Brazil, where Lula was born into rural poverty in the 1940s, a 114-year-old retiree called Josefa Pereira da Conceição went to vote wearing a red T-shirt emblazoned with Lula’s face and the slogan “Strength of the people”.
Election experts are still crunching the numbers to fully understand how Lula pulled off his unprecedented fightback, finding 10.3m extra votes between the first and second rounds.

Explanations include a sharp increase in welfare benefits on the eve of the vote; an extraordinary digital mobilisation involving a pro-Lula WhatsApp group that grew from 50,000 to nearly 11m members in less than a month; and a student-led street rebellion in which millions of citizens protested across Brazil.

Some believe elderly people were also crucial, noting how 1.4 million of the 3 million extra voters who took part in the second round after skipping the first were over 70. Pre-election polls suggested such voters were more inclined to vote for Lula.

Speaking at Lula’s victory celebration, the former minister Simone Tebet called the result a cross-generational triumph which sent a message to the democratic world. “It is possible to resist fascism – all you need to do is mobilise society,” Tebet declared, claiming: “Young people hit the streets and golden-agers saved our democracy.”

The political journalist José Roberto de Toledo said there was concrete evidence of higher turnout among older voters in the runoff, particularly those aged 60 to 79. Voting is only mandatory in Brazil for those aged 18 to 69.

“The images [of elderly people voting] aren’t misleading: they reveal a phenomenon that isn’t just an isolated case. It’s not some made-up story or a staged example. It really happened – and it was a movement you can measure statistically,” Toledo said of the images suggesting an unusually large number of older voters.

That said, Toledo believed the swing to Lula was explained mostly by fear, not age. Voting data suggested many people who backed Lula in the runoff had previously voted for Bolsonaro’s rightwing adversaries, hoping to protest against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), which has governed for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.
In the runoff, faced with a straight choice between Lula, a familiar and predictable figure even for detractors, and Bolsonaro, who represented a leap into the unknown, many preferred the former.

“A protest vote in the first round [became] a safety vote or a lower-risk vote in the second – even if it wasn’t a happy vote,” said Toledo, who believed Bolsonaro alienated many voters with his “arrogant” behaviour after winning the first round.

Particularly damaging was the rightwinger’s authoritarian-sounding vow to “re-democratise” the already democratic country – something Toledo suspected stoked fears that Bolsonaro aspired to be “the emperor of Brazil”.

Even before those remarks, Soares fretted over the direction Brazil might take under Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

“His father wanted to stage a coup … and stay on as president, just like Getúlio [Vargas did in 1937],” recalled the great-grandmother, who was 12 at the time and lived through the subsequent eight years of dictatorial rule.
Marques, a 51-year-old food entrepreneur, said his grandmother-in-law was also critical of how Jair Bolsonaro undermined vaccination efforts during the Covid pandemic, when 700,000 Brazilians died.

“She’s got three great-grandchildren … and she understands she’s nearing the end of her life. But she’s worried about the country, about her family and about future generations,” said Marques, becoming visibly emotional as he recalled watching Soares exercise her democratic right, perhaps for the last time.

“It was so moving to see her strength and desire [to vote] … We felt she had an intuition, or something telling her she needed to be part of this … She doesn’t know if she’ll get another chance,” added Marques, whose 85-year-old father, Helço Muniz, also voted Lula – in his case for the first time.

Sitting in her armchair overlooking Rio’s Guanabara Bay, five days after the election, Soares voiced excitement that Lula would soon start his fourth and final term. “I’ve been fond of him ever since he was poor,” she said of the lathe operator turned president, who first took office as president in 2003. “He was poor and he became rich, but he carried on being a simple man.”
Occasionally, Soares’s memory betrayed her and she needed reminding that Lula had pulled off one of modern history’s greatest democratic comebacks. “But that’s wonderful!” she beamed.
Reminded of Lula’s feat, Soares predicted Bolsonaro would flee abroad.
“He’s already gone!” her granddaughter, Poliana Soares Jordão, 46, told her. “His dad’s in prison and he’s fled.”

Soares, who has lived through four coups, 16 presidential elections and four Lula wins, was not surprised. “He must have gone to the US, then,” the centenarian guessed, correctly. “He’d been getting ready for that for a while, hadn’t he?”

articles.title: Repairing the legacy of slavery: what are campaigners calling for?
articles.summary: Debate has focused on cash payments, but advocates say reparatory justice must address much more than money
body: The debate in much of the British media over reparations has focused almost entirely on cash payments: how much Britain might owe for its role in transatlantic enslavement, who should pay and whether people today should be held responsible for the actions of those who came before them.
But some campaigners warn that this narrow focus overlooks the broader goals of the reparations movement.

Eleanor Shearer, a senior research fellow at Common Wealth, said: “I think we’re missing the root of the word itself, which is repair. It’s about this idea that something has been broken, continues to be broken and we need to work together to fix and to heal.

“And that’s why I think that the narrow focus on money is unhelpful. If you listen to community activists here in the UK, in the Caribbean, what people are asking for is so much more expansive than that.”

Others have emphasised the distinction between reparatory justice and development assistance. Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, said: “We have to understand the specificities of reparatory justice as distinct from general sustainable development goals. They’re shaping the discussion only within the frame of sustainable development goals.”
The problem, he suggested, was that this framing allowed the UK to take a discretionary approach, in contrast to the obligation of a reparatory framework.
But most campaigners agree that there is no version of reparations which amounts to a simple cash transfer. Here are three ways that this broader version of reparatory justice could work in practice.
The most prominent framework for reparation is the Caribbean Community (Caricom) 10-point reparations plan, which sets out demands ranging from healthcare and education to economic development.
Caricom’s revised manifesto explicitly links climate justice to the legacy of colonialism, arguing that plantation economies and centuries of extraction have left the region particularly vulnerable.

“There’s a framework around reparations that is interpreted as punitive. So ‘Let’s go and punish you for the things you did’,” Marvin Rees, the former mayor of Bristol, said. “But actually, there’s another way of looking at the whole question of saying sorry and receiving forgiveness … It’s a process that restores relationships that leaves all parties stronger.”
Related: ‘Reparations now’: King and Burnham face protests at Antigua Commonwealth summit
He believes reparations could therefore take the form of enabling the delivery of “top-class, net zero, climate-resilient infrastructure”, including roads and housing.

Rees argued that there is also a migration dimension. He said leaders including Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, and the mayor of Freetown in Sierra Leone, Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr, have spoken to him about the loss of skilled workers from their countries.
“If we help countries deliver the infrastructure – good homes, energy systems, resilient flood defence, cooling in the summer – people won’t leave,” he said.

“It offers an opportunity to blend the conversation on reparatory justice into the other global priorities that we have helped to shape on climate development, and a management of a just system to manage the movement of people.”

For campaigners in Britain, one longstanding demand is for a national commission to investigate the country’s involvement in slavery and colonialism, examine their present-day consequences and then recommend measures to address them.

Esther Stanford-Xosei, a longstanding reparations campaigner and legal scholar, said: “I’m advocating for a commission of inquiry because I feel that there’s too much of a jump to solutions without us even having the national dialogue. And that includes not just those of us who are calling for reparations and our allies who support the call; it also includes the right of the British public, the wider public, to understand what the issues are.”
Shearer, who also supports a truth-telling process, pointed to how little is taught about transatlantic slavery and the British empire in schools.

“This is particularly important for communities here in the UK because of the complete lack of any forum to talk about what the empire really did to them, to their ancestors, what it’s still doing to their communities and what repair would look like in those communities,” she said.
Caricom has called for the return of objects held in European collections to allow Caribbean communities to engage with histories and knowledge that have often been inaccessible to them.
Its manifesto proposes cultural exchanges, support for artists and scholars and programmes reconnecting descendants of enslaved Africans with their ancestral communities.

Stanford-Xosei has also called for the opening of colonial archives held by the royal family and other British institutions. “We don’t have access to the records … So, even to find out our own history, we’re denied proper access to that. And we don’t get the truth,” she said.

For Shearer, repair also means reclaiming the stories told about slavery and emancipation in arts and culture. “It’s important to kind of be proud of that heritage as well,” she said, pointing to examples of resistance such as the Haitian Revolution. “Communities being able to take more ownership over their history, their stories and shape public understandings and the collective consciousness of those histories, I think that’s the role for the arts.”

articles.title: Met settles claim brought by Palestine activist ‘treated like a criminal’ during arrest
articles.summary: Tej Singh Bhandal, 68, was detained at train station under terrorism law in ‘creeping criminalisation of protest action’
body: The Metropolitan police have settled a claim brought by a 68-year-old pro-Palestinian activist who accused the force of treating him “like a criminal” when he was arrested under anti-terrorism legislation.
Tej Singh Bhandal was returning to the UK on Eurostar this year when police pulled him from a queue at St Pancras International station in London.
After refusing to give authorities the pin code to his mobile phone, he was arrested under schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000, he said.
He spent several hours in police detention, and brought a legal challenge over his arrest. The Met has agreed to settle the claim. They also agreed to settle the claim.

Bhandal’s lawyers said Scotland Yard accepted that supporting and funding lawful political protest organisations – naming the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement and the Palestine Solidarity Campaign – did not automatically establish a link to terrorism.
The Met said it had apologised toBhandal and was carefully reviewing the circumstances of the case.
Bhandal described his arrest as “incredibly humiliating” and “an abuse of power”.
“I was handcuffed and led through the station in full view of the public. I felt like the tabloid newspaper stereotype of a person of colour, and I was treated like a criminal,” he told PA.

Bhandal, who is involved with the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, was arrested in 2025 as part of a police investigation into a Palestine Action-linked incident at the Elbit Systems factory in Bristol. He was questioned by counter-terrorism police over four days, during which his house was searched and his devices seized, but was released with no further action taken.
He said he believed an “intelligence flag” was placed against his name after the incident, leading to his arrest at St Pancras.

The Met’s decision to settle Bhandal’s claim came as more than two dozen protesters were arrested outside the supreme court on Wednesday while an appeal was being heard against the ban on Palestine Action.
He said people were being “singled out by the authorities for activism” and that “the creeping criminalisation of protest action is a consequence of government policy.”.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “We accept that an examination of a 68-year-old man under schedule 7 to the Terrorism Act 2000, on 2 June at St Pancras station, and his subsequent arrest, did not meet the requirements of the legislation. We have apologised to the individual concerned over this.
“Schedule 7 is a key power in protecting the borders of the UK and remains a vital tool in our efforts to counter the terrorist threat and keep the public safe.

“We will carefully review the circumstances of this case and take forward any lessons learned to ensure these powers are exercised lawfully, effectively and in a way that means the public can have confidence and trust in the work we do.”
Alex Kenney, a civil liberties lawyer at Hodge Jones & Allen, which acted for Bhandal, said “adequate safeguards” were essential to prevent the “arbitrary” use of anti-terrorism laws.
“Our hope is that Tej’s case leads to more stringent adherence to the statutory obligations under the Terrorism Act, and changes how the police conduct themselves in future,” she said.

articles.title: Activists across Europe prepare two days of protests against datacentres
articles.summary: More than 100 campaign groups will join together in 15 countries this week to call for a halt to major AI projects
body: Protesters across Europe are planning two days of action against datacentres this week with demonstrations taking place in 15 countries.

More than 100 groups are joining together for the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday. They are calling for a moratorium on large projects, citing environmental and social costs that “we can no longer afford”.

Datacentres have become a lightning rod for concerns over artificial intelligence, given their role in developing and operating the cutting-edge technology. In the US midterm elections this week, opponents of datacentres were among the biggest winners for the Democrats.

Actions across the two days include: a protest outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw; a march in Dublin; a demonstration outside a Microsoft datacentre in Denmark; a “teach-in” near the site of a planned datacentre in Amsterdam; and an event in the Brick Lane area of east London, where a datacentre development has met local opposition.
Owen Espley, the campaign’s coordinator, said communities in the US and Europe are sending a message about data centres.

“Communities and civil society from across Europe are rising up to stop dirty data centres where they live and demand their politicians impose moratoria on large-scale data centre developments,” he said. “The US mid-term results reflect the concerns communities both sides of the Atlantic share about the harms of large-scale data centres.”
Organisers expect attendance at the European events to range from a handful at some to several hundred at larger gatherings such as in Brick Lane and in Dublin.
Groups backing the protests include Friends of the Earth, Greenpeace and Foxglove, a London-based campaign for “a fairer tech future”.
Related: Will it be AI or the climate crisis that ends humanity? We can make it neither | Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks

A key factor in national and local opposition to datacentres is their impact on the environment. By 2030, carbon dioxide emissions from AI datacentres will be six times the 2023 level, according to research by the Öko-Institut of Germany. In the UK, energy use by AI datacentres could cause the emission of up to 123m tonnes of CO2 – about as much as generated by 2.7 million people – over the next 10 years.

Various social impacts are listed by the pan-European campaign, from the impact of chatbots on mental health to the threat of AI eliminating jobs and the prioritisation of datacentres over housing. The tech industry argues that datacentres create jobs during construction and operation, and drive growth by supporting the development and deployment of AI.

About 250 global datacentre projects exceeding 100 megawatts in energy demand – equivalent to about 300,000 homes per project – were announced between 2021 and 2024, with North American schemes dominating the waiting list.
In the UK alone, there are 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the power grid, representing 73 gigawatts of demand compared with the entire country’s peak energy demand of 45GW.

articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
articles.summary: Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
body: The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.

Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”

Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”

Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Related: ‘Hong Kong is at a crossroads’: inside prison with the student who took on Beijing

Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

articles.title: Ministers to target ‘wild west’ of ebikes blocking pavements
articles.summary: Exclusive: Consultation led by Department for Transport will consider parking standards, fleet sizes and insurance requirements
body: Ministers are seeking to end the “wild west” of parked ebikes blocking pavements, as they attempt to crack down on antisocial behaviour such as cyclists jumping red lights.

The consultation, led by the Department for Transport, will aim to establish national standards on issues including parking, ending the current patchwork of agreements between individual bike companies and councils.

While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes – such as those operated by Lime, Forest and Voi – can only be left in designated parking bays, elsewhere the rules are looser, prompting complaints about bikes blocking pavements, particularly for wheelchair users, people with pushchairs and those with impaired vision.
It will also look at antisocial and illegal riding, for example, people jumping lights or the use of bikes by those who are underage or drunk.
Related: Badly parked ebikes in London are a menace – but other cities have shown us the solution | Agustin Guilisasti

The plans will also examine guidelines for fleet sizes to ensure certain areas are not overcrowded and possible requirements for operators to have insurance, so someone hit by a rider on a hired ebike can claim compensation.

Another part of the consultation will look at whether councils and mayors should be given powers over the fees charged to rent bikes, and whether companies should share data to improve enforcement and transport planning.

Since arriving in the UK in 2018, shared ebike systems, of which Lime is by some way the biggest, have expanded rapidly, especially in London. More than 2.6 million Britons used an ebike share scheme in the year to September 2025, according to one estimate.

There is evidence that shared ebikes are used by a broader demographic range of riders than traditional bikes, in part because of the electric assistance, but also because they do not require somewhere secure to park.

The DfT argues that the bikes are growing in importance for urban transport, but that the lack of any central oversight has created difficulties, noting that the companies themselves have called for more regulation.

The proposed changes would be “a small but important everyday fix to make our streets safer”, Andy Burnham said. The prime minister added: “Ebikes can make getting around that bit easier, but when they block pavements or are used irresponsibly they can be a real frustration.
“I want to sort that by giving communities more control over where they are parked and making sure companies and riders play by the rules.”

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, said: “Shared ebike schemes have revolutionised the way people travel around our towns and cities. They are easy to use, get us active and help reduce emissions, but we need to make sure they work with the communities where they operate.
“That’s why we are taking decisive action to give local leaders the power to stop nuisance parking, tackle antisocial behaviour and make journeys safer.”

There are parallel efforts in London under which the DfT would devolve power to the mayor, Sadiq Khan, and Transport for London to unify ebike regulations, which are currently the responsibility of individual boroughs and vary significantly.

Khan said: “The ‘wild west’ approach to dockless ebikes cannot continue. While these services are helping thousands more Londoners to cycle, their rapid growth has also brought challenges around safety, inconsiderate parking and the lack of data needed to properly manage them.

“I’ve been calling for powers to better manage dockless ebike schemes since 2017, when the first schemes arrived in London, so I welcome the government’s plans to give cities the powers they need to do this.”

articles.title: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.summary: Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books
body: From inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.
Related: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.

To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”
The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.
On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion, his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.

Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.
Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.

“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.
In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.
“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.

Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.
On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.

Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.

Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile. There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.
Related: ‘Hong Kong is at a crossroads’: inside prison with the student who took on Beijing
“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.
“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”
In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.
He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.
Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.
“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.
Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.
“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

articles.title: Has Britain finally pulled off a diplomatic victory in the row over reparations?
articles.summary: A formal apology over slavery without direct reparations will give the UK the moral high ground but no legal liability
body: A beach in Antigua is not the ideal place for a prime minister to be photographed less than a week after his first budget where the focus was the crushing cost-of-living crisis.

Add to the beachside cocktail a row about reparations for the British role in the slave trade, one of the favoured punching bags of the right-wing press, and it becomes easy to understand why Andy Burnham was wary of even attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting.

But behind the scenes, Foreign Office officials are convinced they have pulled off a quiet diplomatic victory – but one which will take some time to bear fruit. A clear offer of an apology, which will now be worked on behind the scenes, and a path for the summit to move on from a prominent focus on reparations, which had driven many leaders from countries where that subject is not high on the agenda to avoid it altogether.
Caribbean leaders, on the other hand, reject the idea that the reparations debate drowns out other subjects – instead arguing that it is a vital mechanism for breaking new ground.

Last week, Barbadian prime minister Mia Mottley told the Guardian: “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree.” She cited investment in health and education and fairer debt as some of those issues.

It is in that context that Ed Miliband had told officials that the UK could not work from the same playbook as usual for Chogm by simply demanding the issue was not on the agenda. His view was that even if direct reparations remained ruled out, the UK should put something substantive on the table, like the formal apology, and use its upcoming presidency of the G20 to start a serious conversation about debt restructuring.

Before the summit, one sceptical official said they could judge the health of the Commonwealth by weighing the number of middle powers who decided to attend. On paper, there are still powerful world leaders from counties such as Australia and Canada willing to make the trip – but crucially not from some of the world’s most important economies and regional powers like India, Malaysia, Singapore, Pakistan or South Africa.

It is difficult for a British prime minister to swerve a summit where King Charles is attending. But that, according to reports, was the plan of Keir Starmer before he was ousted. He had planned to send his then-deputy David Lammy in his place, after feeling he was ambushed unfairly with a reparations row at the last summit in Samoa in 2024.

There are still many diplomats across the Commonwealth who share Starmer’s view – that the summit is a waste of their time. One Commonwealth diplomat said: “We know that the royal family values the Commonwealth, but soon that will not be enough to keep it going.”

Lammy commissioned an internal review after Samoa, which suggested that Chogm needed a radical rethink and should be far less frequent than every two years. Any decision on such a change would ultimately sit with the Commonwealth secretariat, not the UK government.
The review proposed an investment summit – which might have a draw for some other middle powers – and a cultural gathering every four to five years linked to events like the Commonwealth Games.

But Miliband wanted to give the gathering another chance to have a meaningful role. When he entered the Foreign Office, allies say he wanted to preserve and elevate the Commonwealth as a political force, despite the pessimism, believing it would be in the UK’s interest to be in a grouping that represents one-third of the world’s people – and in a forum away from powers like China and Russia. The US is also unable to dominate any of its proceedings.

But crucial to that was a path to enable the gathering to move away from being dominated by the issue of reparations – and towards issues like investment, trade and climate change. Miliband’s view – similar to his approach on Israel and Palestine – was that the issue of reparations and Britain’s history had to be confronted head-on rather than angrily dismissed.

The apology will be worked on over the months ahead to try to reach a common understanding and satisfaction which does not leave Britain legally compromised. But few take the view that is a serious risk. One senior former government lawyer, who has worked on international cases, said offering an apology was “risk free” when it came to the idea of potential compensation. “Simply saying sorry does not give any rights of itself,” they said. “It doesn’t push you into a corner, legally.”

Government strategists believe this apology will eventually lead to a more productive forum than allowing the summit to drift. “Two years ago, the Keir Starmer approach was to just say we’re not talking about it,” one said.

“The PM and Ed Miliband took a view that that is just not tenable, that you have to show willingness to do the right thing, which is to open this apology discussion because it’s morally the right thing to do.

“And more than that, there’s a hard-nosed argument to that if we can show Commonwealth countries we can deal with this, then we can move forward with them. We won’t be cowed by the right on this. Mainstream public opinion supports our sensible, moral position.”

Cynics believe it will never be enough and that the gathering cannot be redeemed. “I think that the current structures that the Commonwealth has are unsalvageable and I think that you can see that from the attendance lists,” said Ben Judah, Lammy’s former adviser.

“Many of the powers just don’t want to be part of a kind of unhappy, fractious conversation about the past, which generates this ugly row in the UK about Britain’s identity. Putin recently had 22 African leaders in Moscow. The Russians can do a more successful business summit with the global South.”
There is a significant amount at stake in the months ahead, and Miliband’s diplomatic success cannot be fairly judged until the next summit – and who can be convinced to host it.

For now, diplomats will begin to work on the text of an apology, while the UK will hope to move the focus on to debt, on which Gordon Brown will take the lead ahead of the G20 summit, to convince leaders that should be their primary ask and that it is the biggest hindrance to development.

The G20 in Manchester is a far cry – and in a different world – from the 2005 Gleneagles summit which cancelled the debt of many poorer nations. But there is a hope that Brown can convene a serious offer on debt restructuring in time to announce it when Britain hosts the global gathering.

articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.summary: Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification
body: The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
Related: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

articles.title: New Zealand heads for election cliffhanger with minor party cast as kingmaker
articles.summary: Polls show neither major party will have enough seats to form government, meaning the fate could fall on centrist minor party, Opportunity
body: The final polls ahead of New Zealand’s election show a knife-edge path to power, with neither the ruling right-wing coalition or opposition left bloc able to form a government without the support of a newcomer centrist party.

New Zealanders will vote on 7 November, concluding a six-week campaign defined by the high costs of living, a wobbling healthcare system, political tit-for-tats over gangs, personal attacks, and complex vote-splitting strategies.

“A lot of [the campaign] has been quite negative in the last few weeks and I think … most people are kind of sick of it and ready for it to be over,” said Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington.

A final push from National – the major party in the ruling right bloc – and the opposition Labour party has done little to budge their cratering popularity, with both parties sitting below 30% in polls released this week.
Related: ‘So hacked off’: as election nears, New Zealanders despair at the main parties – and Opportunity knocks

The 1News-Verian poll, released Tuesday, has prime minister Christopher Luxon’s National on 30%, with Chris Hipkins-led Labour on 29%. A Taxpayers’ Union/Curia poll had National on 28.9% and Labour on 28.4%.

New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) system requires two votes – one for a party and one for a local electorate candidate. Small parties often hold the balance of power. In 2023, National got 38% of the vote and needed the New Zealand First and Act parties to form a government.
Minor parties are continuing to scoop up votes from National and Labour.
Across both polls left-wing Greens are polling between 14 and 16%, the libertarian Act party 10%, the populist New Zealand First party between 8 and 9% and Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) about 1%.

The numbers indicate that neither left or right bloc will have enough seats to form a government, so their fate could fall to the centrist minor party, Opportunity, which polls show could clear the 5% threshold to become kingmaker.

The Opportunity party, led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, 38, has said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of votes. However, Luxon has ruled out working with Opportunity numerous times, saying its proposed land tax runs contrary to National’s “no new taxes” pledge.
Should he keep his promise, National faces the possibility of being the first one-term National-led government since the party was founded in 1936.

In another late blow to Luxon’s hopes, unemployment unexpectedly rose to a fresh 11-year high, hitting 5.7% in the September quarter, according to data released Tuesday. And according to the most recent Ipsos issues monitor, released on Monday, most people think Labour is the best party to deal with nine out of the 10 most pressing everyday concerns of voters.

Polls are also indicating the potential of several overhang seats, where a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote. If that occurs, more seats will be added to parliament and could dictate which coalition can form a government.
More than one million New Zealanders have voted early this year – already up about 30% compared to the 2023 election, which Greaves suspects could be down to the closeness of the race.
Related: In New Zealand’s bellwether seat, what are locals thinking as a knife-edge poll looms?
But it could take weeks for New Zealand to know the shape of its government, Greaves says.
“There’s two possibilities here: one is that there’s a clear winner at the end of the night, and then they set about negotiating,” she says.

But if there is no clear winner, parties must wait for the final count, due 27 November. If special votes, which includes overseas votes, add seats to a party, or an overhang is created, that could “change the whole map of the house”.
Either way, the future government is going to have a “tough ride” ahead, Greaves says.
“Generally, it does seem like it will be a really challenging time for whoever ends up having to govern.”
